questions.q: N-Phenylhydroxylamine is warmed with aqueous H₂SO₄. The main product is:
questions.explain: In the Bamberger rearrangement the OH leaves nitrogen as water and a new OH arrives at the ring carbon para to nitrogen, giving p-aminophenol. Nitrosobenzene needs an oxidant such as dichromate, and aniline comes from over-reduction of nitrobenzene.

questions.q: In the Bamberger rearrangement, the OH group of the product 4-aminophenol comes from:
options: Water of the solvent, which attacks the para carbon
The original N–OH group, by an intramolecular shift to the para carbon
questions.explain: After O-protonation, water leaves and solvent water attacks the para carbon. Drawing an intramolecular OH shift from N to the ring is the classic mistake.

questions.q: If the Bamberger rearrangement of N-phenylhydroxylamine is carried out in hydrochloric acid instead of sulphuric acid:
options: The reaction does not occur at all
questions.explain: Chloride competes with water as the nucleophile at the ring carbons, giving chloroanilines. The sulphate anion is a poor nucleophile, which is why H₂SO₄ gives 4-aminophenol cleanly.

questions.q: Which electron-deficient species is formed when water leaves the O-protonated N-phenylhydroxylamine in the textbook mechanism?
options: A nitrenium ion, C₆H₅NH⁺, with positive charge delocalised to ortho and para carbons
A phenyl carbocation formed by loss of NH₂OH
questions.explain: Loss of water from C₆H₅NH–OH₂⁺ gives the nitrenium ion C₆H₅NH⁺; its charge is best stabilised at the para carbon, which water attacks. N-protonation is favoured but leads nowhere; only O-protonation is productive.
